messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 56
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Musician
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 71

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Violence: Violence, Visual/Bodily Cues: Blood, Olfactory (Cologne/Perfume): A specific perfume or cologne
  Maladaptive Strategies: Suppress Anger: never allow myself to feel or express anger, Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform, Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
  Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
  Memory: Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Viktor Hale is a 56-year-old married musician of European descent who presents with a PCL-5 score of 71 following a sexual assault that occurred approximately eighteen months ago. He was assaulted by a male authority figure — a well-established producer who had invited him to a private studio session under professional pretenses. The assault took place in a confined space, and Viktor recalls with terrible clarity the man's physical weight, the sight of blood from where his hand struck a surface, and the overwhelming presence of a particular cologne — heavy, cedar-based — that the producer wore. What he cannot reconstruct is the sequence of events that connected those fragments: there are stretches of the encounter that remain entirely blank to him, and he has never been able to tell himself a coherent story of what happened that night. He knows what he knows in pieces, and the pieces do not form a whole.

In the months that followed, Viktor found that certain sensory moments could collapse the distance between then and now without warning. The sight of any physical altercation — even a shove between strangers on the street — would drop him immediately into a state of raw vigilance. Blood, encountered during a minor kitchen accident or glimpsed on a television screen, produced the same effect. Most destabilising of all was scent: on one occasion a fellow musician at a rehearsal wore a cologne with a similar cedar note, and Viktor left the room without explanation and did not return. These triggers fed directly into a sustained state of threat — his nervous system, already primed, would escalate rapidly into irritability, angry outbursts that frightened him as much as those around him, and a hypervigilance to sudden movements by others that made ensemble playing feel genuinely dangerous.

The fragmented, incoherent quality of his memory has become one of the central engines of his distress. Because he cannot narrate what happened — even privately, even to himself — he cannot locate the danger in the past. The memory exists not as a story with a beginning and an end but as a set of live sensory charges, and this means that his triggers carry the full weight of the original threat rather than the weight of something remembered. The incompleteness of the memory also drives the threat appraisal directly: Viktor is certain, in a way he cannot fully articulate, that what he cannot remember is worse than what he can, and this certainty keeps his body in a permanent state of preparation for something unspecified and therefore inescapable.

In response to this sustained threat, Viktor began organising his life around containment. He identified the places where he felt safe — his home studio, the back garden, one particular corner of a café two blocks from his house — and he has not meaningfully left that geography in months. He stopped attending the open sessions and informal gatherings that had been the social fabric of his professional life, avoiding the musicians, producers, and industry contacts he had known before the assault. He has never allowed himself to feel or express anger, suppressing it the moment it rises, convinced that if he lets it surface he will become something he cannot control. He avoids any situation involving authority figures — managers, venue owners, anyone in a position of institutional power — which has effectively ended his ability to negotiate his own career. His wife has noticed that he is no longer the person she married, and the distance between them has grown in proportion to the territory he has ceded to avoidance.

What is particularly insidious is the way his strategies have closed off the possibility of resolution. By pushing the memory away each time it begins to surface before it can complete itself, Viktor ensures that the fragments remain raw and unprocessed. The suppression of anger and the avoidance of social contact mean that he never encounters the triggers in a context that might allow them to lose their charge; instead, when they do break through — a sudden movement in his peripheral vision, a scent on the air — they arrive with full force and confirm his belief that nowhere, and no one, is safe.

What finally brought Viktor to seek help was a session he had been trying to complete for weeks: a recording he had promised a close friend, done in his own home studio, that he has been unable to finish because he cannot remain in the room long enough. He is most afraid that whatever he cannot remember will eventually surface and destroy him. What he is hoping for, more quietly, is that someone might help him find a way to carry this that does not require surrendering everything he has built.
